description: A cherry is the fruit of many plants of the genus Prunus, and is a fleshy drupe. Commercial cherries are obtained from cultivars of several species, such as the sweet Prunus avium and the sour Prunus cerasus.

data_sources.notes: height_cm corrected from 1500 to 300 (GitHub issue #159): confirmed the 1500 (15m) value is present verbatim in openfarm-crops-rescue's own cached crops.json (data/.cache/openfarm-crops-rescue/crops.json), not something introduced by this project's ETL - a units/data-quality error at the original source, implausible for a garden fruit tree (standard/dwarf sour or sweet cherry trees are typically 200-500cm). No usable alternate value was recoverable from Trefle either (data/.cache/trefle/cherry.json's average_height/maximum_height are both null, a known gap - see data/CLAUDE.md). Set to 300cm as a reasonable estimate pending a better source, matching this dataset's own convention for other garden-scale fruit trees (apple.json and green-bartlett-pear.json both use height_cm=300).
growing_information text sourced from 'Home Vegetable Gardening'
life_cycle='perennial' inferred by Ollama; reasoning: Cherry trees are typically grown as perennials in a home garden setting.

is_edible corrected from false to true (GitHub issue #165): edible_parts=['fruit'] was already populated, a direct contradiction with is_edible=false, and no is_toxic flag or toxicity_notes explained the discrepancy - a full-dataset audit found this affecting 120 plants (grown from an earlier 25-plant spot-check once backlog #133's edible_parts backfill widened coverage), all of them unambiguous real food/herb/fruit crops.

height_cm=300 kept as-is, not reverted to 1500 (GitHub issue #189, revisiting #159): confirmed real per-cultivar height variance already exists elsewhere in this dataset's own openfarm-crops-rescue source data (fuji-apple=360, golden-delicious-apple/granny-smith-apple=450 vs. the generic apple=300; rainier-cherry=750 vs. this generic cherry record's original 1500), consistent with real rootstock/cultivar-driven size differences in cherry/apple trees (roughly: dwarf rootstock ~200-400cm, semi-vigorous ~400-600cm, standard/seedling rootstock unpruned ~800-1500cm+ - general horticultural knowledge, not independently re-verified via a live source this pass, no WebFetch/WebSearch available in this session). So 1500 isn't necessarily a units error as #159 originally framed it - it's plausible for an unpruned standard-rootstock tree. However this generic species-level 'cherry' record has no cultivar/rootstock qualifier to hang that on (unlike rainier-cherry, a specific cultivar with its own consistent height/spread/row-spacing figures), and the source data itself is inconsistent about whether a bare species-level heightCm means 'typical garden tree' or 'unpruned wild maximum' (apple's own generic record is LOWER than its named cultivars, the opposite pattern from cherry) - so no single number here can be trusted as more authoritative than another. 300cm stays as the representative 'typical garden tree, unspecified rootstock' default, consistent with this dataset's sibling generic tree records (apple, green-bartlett-pear, sour-cherry all use 300). The real range is documented here rather than in a new structured field - height_cm as a single number has no way to represent rootstock-driven variance, and adding one (e.g. height_cm_min/height_cm_max) is a schema-impact decision flagged for backend-developer/product-owner, not made here.

growing_information.text:
Cherries have one advantage over the other fruits—they give quicker returns. But, as far as my experience goes, they are not as long-lived. The sour type is hardier, at least north of New Jersey, than the sweet. It will probably pay to try a few of the new and highly recommended varieties. Of the established sorts Early Richmond is a good early, to be followed by Montmorency and English Morello. Windsor is a good sweet cherry, as are also Black Tartarian, Sox, Wood and Yellow Spanish.

All the varieties mentioned above are proved sorts. But the lists are being added to constantly, and where there is a novelty strongly recommended by a reliable nurseryman it will often pay to try it out—on a very small scale at first.

Sour cherries are more easily grown than the sweet varieties, and are less subject to the attacks of fruit enemies. Sweet cherries are troubled by the curculio, or fruit-worm, which attacks also peaches and plums. Cherries and plums may be sprayed, when most of the blossoms are off, with a strong arsenate of lead solution, 5 to 8 lbs. to 100 gals. water. In addition to this treatment, where the worms have once got a start, the beetles may be destroyed by spreading a sheet around and beneath the tree, and every day or so shaking or jarring them off into it, as described below.

Cherries offer quicker returns compared to other fruits but may have a shorter lifespan. Sour cherries are hardier and easier to grow north of New Jersey, particularly varieties like Early Richmond (good early variety), Montmorency, and English Morello. For sweet cherries, consider Windsor, Black Tartarian, Sox, Wood, and Yellow Spanish. When selecting varieties, it's beneficial to try new recommendations from reliable nurserymen on a small scale initially. Sour cherries are less susceptible to pests compared to sweet varieties, which can be troubled by the curculio or fruit-worm. To manage this pest, spray trees with a strong arsenate of lead solution (5-8 kg per 379 L water) after most blossoms have fallen. Additionally, place a sheet around and beneath the tree, shaking it daily to dislodge beetles into the sheet for disposal.
